findings.issue: For PayloadMode.OfficeKey and PayloadMode.Session the content key is fully deterministic: SubKey() = HKDF-SHA256(rootKey, info="wakeel.container|<kind>") with an empty salt and no per-container randomness. Every .wakeel-sync packet ever produced by one office therefore encrypts under one and the same AES-256-GCM key, and Aead.EncryptStream picks a fresh random 96-bit nonce per frame. Frame counts are small enough that a nonce collision is practically unreachable (~10^5-10^6 frames over the product's life vs. the 2^48 birthday bound), but a GCM nonce repeat under a long-lived office key is catastrophic when it happens (authentication-key recovery), and the office key is issued once by the administrator and never rotated. Same reasoning applies to the pairing session key.
findings.fix: Add a required 16-byte random field (e.g. `KeySalt`) to ContainerManifest, fill it in ContainerWriter.Write from RandomBytes.Next(16), and change ContainerKeySource.SubKey to Hkdf.DeriveKey(rootKey, Aead.KeySize, keySalt, $"wakeel.container|{token}") on both the write and the read path (the reader already has the manifest before it derives). The salt is inside the signed manifest, so it cannot be rewritten; manifest version can stay 1 since nothing has shipped.

findings.issue: PairingAccept.EnsureTrusted (line 214) checks that Body.PhoneCertificate.Body.DeviceId equals Body.PhoneDeviceId and verifies org->pc->phone, but never checks that the issued phone certificate actually carries the phone's own Ed25519Pub / X25519Pub. A phone that runs EnsureTrusted and stores the returned certificate can end up holding a validly-chained certificate bound to someone else's keys; every packet it later signs would be rejected by the far side, and the failure would surface long after pairing, at a point where the user is told only that pairing succeeded. (No privilege escalation: only an already org-certified computer can produce such a file.)
findings.fix: Add the phone's own public keys as parameters (or take the phone DeviceIdentity) and, before returning, compare Body.PhoneCertificate.Body.Ed25519Pub and X25519Pub against them with StringComparison.Ordinal, throwing CryptoException(ErrorCode.BadSignature, ...) on a mismatch. While there, also compare Body.OrgId/Body.OfficeId/Body.PcDeviceId with pc.Body.OrgId/OfficeId/DeviceId so the plain body fields the phone reads cannot disagree with the certificate they are supposed to describe.

findings.issue: PairingAccept.OpenSessionKey (line 264) and OpenOfficeKey (line 271) dereference Body.SealedSessionKey / Body.SealedOfficeKey with no null guard. A pairing-accept file whose JSON is e.g. {"signature":"x"} deserializes with Body = null, so these two methods throw NullReferenceException instead of CryptoException. Round 1 established that every failure from a hostile document must leave this project as a CryptoException (CanonicalJsonTests.An_unreadable_instant_is_reported_as_corrupt_and_nothing_else pins exactly that contract); these two entry points were missed. A caller is expected to call EnsureTrusted first, but nothing enforces the order.
findings.fix: At the top of both methods add `if (Body is null || string.IsNullOrEmpty(Body.SealedSessionKey /* resp. SealedOfficeKey */)) throw new CryptoException(ErrorCode.Corrupt, "The computer's answer is incomplete.");` — the same guard EnsureTrusted already uses.

findings.issue: ContainerEntrySource.IsAcceptableName accepts names that are legal as relative paths but illegal as Windows file names: wildcard characters ("a*b.txt", "a?b"), a trailing '/', and reserved device names. ExtractTo (line 249-250) then hands such a name straight to `new FileStream(target, FileMode.Create, ...)`, which raises a raw IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException rather than a CryptoException, so a hostile manifest can still produce an unexplained fault in the interface. (The path-escape itself is correctly blocked: a reserved name resolves to \\.\CON and fails the rootWithSeparator check.)
findings.fix: In ContainerEntrySource.IsAcceptableName also reject any character in Path.GetInvalidFileNameChars() other than '/', reject a name ending in '/', '.' or ' ', and reject any segment whose name-without-extension matches a DOS device name (CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9, case-insensitively). The reader already applies this same predicate in ValidateShape, so the fix covers both sides at once.

findings.issue: The two administrator-recovery paths report the same situation with different codes. KeyWraps.OpenAsAdmin (line 112) lets the ErrorCode.Tampered from DeviceIdentity.Open escape unchanged (pinned by KeyWrapTests.An_admin_wrap_opens_only_with_the_organisation_keys), while ContainerKeySource.OpenContentKey maps the identical failure to ErrorCode.WrongPassword (pinned by ContainerTests.The_administrator_opens_a_password_backup_without_the_password). The administration tool in B1 will map one code to a user-facing message and be surprised by the other.
findings.fix: Wrap the call in KeyWraps.OpenAsAdmin the way ContainerKeySource does: catch CryptoException when Code == ErrorCode.Tampered and rethrow as CryptoException(ErrorCode.WrongPassword, "These administration keys do not open this wrap.", exception); update the assertion in KeyWrapTests accordingly.

findings.issue: Write() returns the in-memory ContainerManifest built at line 122 with request.Time.GetUtcNow() at full DateTimeOffset precision, but CanonicalJson's UtcInstantConverter truncates instants to milliseconds when it writes the signed bytes. The returned manifest's CreatedAt therefore does not equal the CreatedAt a ContainerReader parses back from the same file whenever the clock carries sub-millisecond ticks. B6 will compare the two when it records what it exported.
findings.fix: Truncate before building the manifest: `var createdAt = new DateTimeOffset(request.Time.GetUtcNow().UtcDateTime.AddTicks(-(now.UtcDateTime.Ticks % TimeSpan.TicksPerMillisecond)), TimeSpan.Zero);` and pass that value into the ContainerManifest constructor, so the returned object and the signed bytes agree exactly.

findings.issue: ReadOne (line 304) copies a whole inner-zip entry into a MemoryStream and only afterwards compares the produced length with expected.Size in CheckEntry. A payload whose inner zip declares a small entry but expands to gigabytes exhausts memory before the check runs. Reaching this requires knowledge of the content key (the office key, the backup password or the recipient device), so it is not remotely triggerable, but it is a free check to add.
findings.fix: In ReadOne, copy through a length-limiting wrapper that throws CryptoException(ErrorCode.Tampered, ...) as soon as more than expected.Size bytes have been written; do the same in ExtractTo, where the same unbounded copy writes to disk.

notes:
VERIFICATION. Ran exactly `dotnet build src/Wakeel.Crypto && dotnet test tests/Wakeel.Crypto.Tests` from D:\AI\Administration2. Build succeeded, 0 Warning(s) / 0 Error(s) under TreatWarningsAsErrors=true. Test run: Failed 0, Passed 168, Total 168, 4 s. Directory.Build.props, Directory.Packages.props and Wakeel.slnx are untouched in `git status`; the only modified/untracked paths under this package's ownership are src/Wakeel.Crypto and tests/Wakeel.Crypto.Tests (other agents' Core/UI changes are present in the tree but were not built). No package was added: the csproj references only NSec.Cryptography and Konscious.Security.Cryptography.Argon2, both already pinned centrally. No git command was run and I modified no file.

SPEC COVERAGE — all nine items are implemented; missing_spec_items is empty. The two owner decisions the builder left open are already settled against him by the governing document: ARCHITECTURE.md §3 now records the 2026-09-15 decisions that the recovery sheet prints 4-4-4-4-5 with the check character at the end of the last group (RecoveryCode.Group matches), and that certificates carry no expiry at all, revocation plus a one-day future-dating limit being the whole mechanism (CertificateChain matches). The extra `issuedAt` in PairingQrPayload is likewise required by ARCHITECTURE §7, not an excess. So open issues 1, 2 and 3 from the builder's report need no owner action; they are closed by the document.

SECURITY REVIEW — I looked specifically for the classes you named and found no high or medium instance. Ordering is right: ContainerReader.Open reads the manifest, validates its shape, hashes the payload, verifies the Ed25519 signature over the labelled sha256(manifest)||sha256(payload), verifies the chain to the organisation root, then checks kind, version and createdAt, and only ReadEntries/ReadEntry/ExtractTo ever touch a content key. The round-1 HIGH is genuinely closed: with VerifyCertificateChain on (the default) a missing or wrong-length OrgSigningPublicKey is a hard BadSignature refusal, and ContainerTests.A_container_from_a_certificate_nobody_issued_is_refused proves a self-issued certificate naming the real organisation does not open. Domain separation is applied to all five signed structures and is proved negatively (a signature over the bare canonical body no longer verifies). The AEAD stream header is inside every frame's associated data, frames are indexed and the final frame is flagged, so truncation, reordering and a rewritten chunk size all fail. Nonces: the one-shot Encrypt takes a fresh random 12 bytes each call, key wraps carry their own nonce with a fresh Argon2 salt per wrap, password containers re-salt on every write (WithFreshSalt), sealed boxes use a fresh ephemeral X25519 pair — the only deterministic key derivation is the office/session sub-key in finding 1. Comparisons that matter are constant-time (Sha256.FixedTimeEquals, PairingRequest.VerifyToken via CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals, AES-GCM tags inside the platform); the hash-hex comparison in CheckEntry is over public integrity data, which is fine. KDF parameters are sound and enforced: Argon2Params.Validate rejects anything below 32 MB, AutoTune starts at 64 MB/3/2, halves only while a probe exceeds 1.5×target and stops at 32 MB, and the RFC 9106 §5.3 Argon2id vector is pinned byte for byte, which also proves the memory unit is kibibytes. X25519 agreement rejects the all-zero shared secret. The path-escape fix is real and double-locked (name rule at manifest-parse time plus a root-prefix check in ExtractTo), and the staging files on both sides are FileMode.CreateNew + FileOptions.DeleteOnClose with the content key zeroed in a finally.

API SHAPE for the other packages looks usable as ARCHITECTURE describes it, with two contract notes B1/B6/B7 must be told. (1) The .wakeel-setup bootstrap has a chicken-and-egg step this package cannot solve for the caller: the organisation signing key arrives inside the setup file, so first-run code must open it with VerifyCertificateChain = false, extract the organisation key and the revocation list, then re-open (or re-verify the producer certificate by hand) before trusting anything. That is a legitimate use of the explicit opt-out, but B1 should do it in one small helper so the opt-out appears exactly once in the product. (2) Nothing here prevents replay of a valid container, and the short pairing code is not consumed anywhere in this project; single-use of the code and packet-id de-duplication are host state and belong to B6/B7 per ARCHITECTURE §6 and §7. The builder's other contract notes (admin copy required for backup/msg/transfer/inventory, PairingAccept.Issue taking the invitation, EnsureTrusted as the phone-side entry point, StagingDirectory under C:\ProgramData\Wakeel) are all correct as stated and match the code.

TESTS assert real behaviour, not tautologies. 152 Fact/Theory attributes expanding to 168 cases, far above the 40 asked for. The negative tests construct genuinely adversarial artefacts — a re-signed manifest naming "..\\outside\\evil.txt", a payload replaced and re-signed with the producer's real key, a self-issued certificate naming the real organisation, an accept message belonging to another invitation — rather than merely flipping a byte and asserting an exception. TimeProvider is used everywhere time matters (FixedClock for wall-clock checks, SteppingClock to force AutoTune fast and slow), so nothing depends on real time. The Argon2 reference vector and the "same secret always renders the same code" test pin cross-device reproducibility, which B7 will need on Android. No Arabic appears anywhere in src/Wakeel.Crypto (verified by codepoint search); the Arabic strings in the test project are payload data, which is right.

VERDICT: accept. Build and tests pass and nothing rises above low. The seven findings are all worth folding in before B1 and B7 build on this, but none of them blocks sign-off, and finding 1 is the only one I would insist on doing before the first container format is considered frozen, because it changes the manifest.
